Boston Dynamics Employees Push Back Against ICE Robot Dog Contract

Internal Disagreement Over Federal Robotics Contract

More than 300 employees at Boston Dynamics have petitioned their executive leadership to halt a deal involving the company’s Spot robot dogs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The petition, which represents approximately 21% of the company's workforce, expresses deep ethical concerns regarding how the technology is utilized by federal agencies. Despite the internal outcry, Boston Dynamics executives have confirmed they will maintain the contract, asserting that the machines are intended for public safety and non-lethal observation.

Scope of the Contract and Capabilities

The contract, valued at $1.3 million, was awarded to Radeco, a Connecticut-based firm, to provide ICE with four quadruped robots branded as "Cerberus." These units are modified versions of the Boston Dynamics Spot platform. According to the federal contract, the devices are intended for "counter-illicit cross-border tunnel operations" and identifying hazardous conditions, such as toxic gas leaks, radiation, or explosive threats. The hardware features 360-degree cameras, thermal imaging, 30-times zoom capabilities, and an optional robotic arm for manipulating objects.

Ethical Concerns and Corporate Response

The petitioning employees argued that the deployment of these robots by ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit creates significant reputational risk and moral conflict for the staff. Concerns were specifically heightened by HSI’s historical role in workplace raids, including a September 2025 operation at a Hyundai Motor Group facility in Georgia—an event that directly impacted colleagues within the broader corporate ecosystem, as Hyundai is the parent company of Boston Dynamics.

In an internal communication, former interim CEO Amanda McMaster defended the deal, stating that the decision aligns with the company’s goal of "ethically advancing intelligent machines in service of humanity." The company maintains that the robots are strictly prohibited from being used as weapons or for intimidation, a policy reinforced by their existing terms of service. A spokesperson noted that Boston Dynamics would take "immediate action," including the termination of licenses and voiding of warranties, should any customer violate these stipulations.

Practical Implications and Verification

For observers and potential employees, this situation highlights the evolving intersection of commercial robotics and federal law enforcement. Readers should note that while the company has stringent anti-weaponization clauses in its terms of sale, the use of these platforms by agencies involved in immigration enforcement remains a point of intense public and internal debate.

  • Confirmed Facts: A $1.3 million contract exists for the provision of four Cerberus (modified Spot) robots to ICE; over 300 Boston Dynamics employees signed a petition against the deal; the company has explicitly rejected the petition and confirmed the deal will proceed.
  • Uncertainties: It remains unclear how this internal friction will impact long-term employee retention or the company's stated goal of creating 1,250 new jobs at its Waltham facility by 2033.
  • Verification: Readers can review the original coverage and the details regarding the scope of the robot modification via the official report at [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/10/boston-dynamics-employees-want-to-block-sale-of-robot-dogs-to-ice/).
